title: 7.3 Psychology of Drawdowns
summary: A drawdown is not just a math event.
bodyHtml:
7.3 Psychology of Drawdowns

Why This Matters

A drawdown is not just a math event.

It is also a behavior test.

If your account grows from USD 1,500 to USD 2,000 and then drops to USD 1,700, you are in a drawdown from your peak.

The money matters. But the bigger danger for many beginners is what happens next:

  • they try to win it back too fast;
  • they freeze and stop taking valid setups;
  • they start bending rules without admitting it.

That is why drawdowns need a plan.

What You Should Understand After This Lesson

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • define drawdown in simple language;
  • identify common emotional responses to losses;
  • use a basic drawdown protocol instead of reacting on impulse.

What a Drawdown Means

A drawdown is the drop from your account peak to a lower point.

Example:

  1. Your account reaches USD 2,000.
  2. It falls to USD 1,700.
  3. The drop is USD 300.

Your review question is not only:

how much did I lose?

It is also:

what is this loss doing to my decision-making?

That second question matters because behavior often gets worse during losing periods.

Why Losses Feel Different

Daniel Kahneman's work and CME's risk-aversion lesson both point to a common human pattern:

  • people dislike losses strongly;
  • after losses, people may make worse risk decisions;
  • they may gamble to avoid accepting the pain of being wrong.

In plain language:

losses can push people into rushed, emotional choices

That is one reason drawdowns are dangerous. They do not only reduce capital. They can distort judgment.

Three Common Drawdown Reactions

Reaction What it looks like Why it is dangerous
Revenge sizing Increasing size to make money back quickly One bad trade can deepen the drawdown
Freezing Refusing to take a valid setup after a losing streak Fear starts controlling execution
Quiet rule-bending Widening stops, forcing trades, or changing rules mid-trade The process becomes unstable

(Table alt-text: A three-row table showing common emotional reactions to drawdowns and why each one is dangerous.)

None of these reactions fixes the real problem. They usually make it worse.

A Basic Drawdown Protocol

When your losses hit a level you already defined in your plan, use a written response.

Step What to do Why it matters
1. Stop Do not place another impulsive trade Creates space between emotion and action
2. Measure Record the drawdown size and recent trade sample Makes the problem concrete
3. Diagnose Check whether the losses came from normal variance or broken rules Tells you what actually needs fixing
4. Reduce pressure Cut size or pause trading for a set time Helps restore discipline
5. Resume carefully Return only when execution quality is stable again Protects the account from repeated mistakes

(Table alt-text: A five-row table showing a basic drawdown protocol from stopping new trades to resuming carefully.)

The point is not to punish yourself. The point is to stop the drawdown from turning into emotional damage.

One Multi-Market Example

Imagine you lose four trades in a row:

  • one in EUR/USD;
  • one in a Nasdaq or S&P 500 product;
  • one in gold;
  • one in Brent crude.

Your weak response might be:

  • double size on the fifth trade;
  • tell yourself the next market "has to" pay you back;
  • jump into another chart with no real setup.

Your stronger response might be:

  • stop trading for the day;
  • review the last four entries in your journal;
  • ask whether the losses came from one broken behavior across all markets or from normal variance;
  • reduce size when you come back.

That second response is not dramatic. It is disciplined.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Trying to Recover in One Trade

Fast recovery thinking often creates even larger losses.

Mistake 2: Confusing Emotion With Information

Feeling urgent does not mean the next trade is better.

Mistake 3: Changing Rules in the Middle of Stress

If you change stops, size, or setups during a drawdown, review becomes harder and risk becomes less controlled.

Mistake 4: Hiding From the Data

If you refuse to review the losses, you lose the chance to fix the real issue.
learningOutcomes: identify common emotional responses to losses;
apply a simple review-first drawdown protocol.

quizItems.prompt: What is a common danger during a drawdown?
quizItems.explanation: The lesson explains that losses often trigger rushed recovery behavior or quiet rule changes.

quizItems.prompt: What is the most disciplined first response to a major drawdown threshold?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stop and review whether the process or behavior changed

correctAnswer.label: B
correctAnswer.text: Stop and review whether the process or behavior changed

quizItems.explanation: The protocol begins with stopping new impulsive trades and diagnosing the cause of the drawdown.
